stimulus.text:
Painting: William B. T. Trego's The March to Valley Forge, December 19, 1777 (painted 1883) shows George Washington on a white horse leading a column of Continental soldiers through snow. The men march in ragged clothes, some barefoot, carrying muskets and a drum, while officers on horseback ride beside them.

Letter: “I am now convinced beyond a doubt, that unless some great and capital change suddenly takes place in that line this Army must inevitably be reduced to one or other of these three things. Starve—dissolve—or disperse, in order to obtain subsistence in the best manner they can.”
—George Washington to Henry Laurens, president of Congress, Valley Forge, December 23, 1777
stimulus.source_note: William B. T. Trego, The March to Valley Forge, December 19, 1777 (1883); George Washington to Henry Laurens, December 23, 1777. Public domain.

source: original; stimuli viewed before writing — Washington to Henry Laurens, December 23, 1777; Trego, The March to Valley Forge, 1883, public domain.

stem: Taken together, the letter and the painting best show how Americans later remembered Valley Forge as

options.text: A winter of heroic endurance that made the army
Proof that Congress had abandoned the army entirely
options.misconception: Congress did not abandon the army; Washington's letter is itself an appeal to Congress for the supplies the army needed.

options.text: The moment France decided to enter the war
options.misconception: France decided to ally after Saratoga in October 1777, not because of the winter at Valley Forge.

options.text: A decisive battle that destroyed the British army
options.misconception: No battle was fought at Valley Forge; the army wintered there, and the British army was not destroyed.

rationales.A: Washington's warning of starvation and Trego's ragged men marching through snow together became the story of suffering endured and an army remade.
rationales.D: Valley Forge was a winter camp, not a battle; no British army was destroyed there.
rationales.B: Washington wrote to Congress to demand action, which is the opposite of Congress having abandoned the army.
rationales.C: France allied after Saratoga, in February 1778; the winter at Valley Forge did not cause that decision.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two sources side by side. A desperate letter about starvation, and a painting, made a century later, of ragged men marching through snow.
2. Ask what the painting adds. Trego did not see the march; he painted what the winter had come to mean — endurance that forged an army.
3. Test the other stories. No battle, no abandonment, and no French decision happened at Valley Forge.
Remember: when a letter and a later painting agree, ask whether they agree on the facts or on the meaning — memory and report are different kinds of truth.
